title: SEOs Are Becoming The Tools Of Their Tools – The AI Slop Backlash via @sejournal, @gregjarboe
content:
Artificial intelligence was supposed to raise the floor for content quality. Instead, the conversation has shifted to something far less flattering. AI slop is everywhere, and the reaction from platforms is no longer subtle. This matters for SEOs because the backlash is aimed at the very tools many practitioners now treat as shortcuts.
The heart of the matter is simple. If AI makes it easier to publish more content, it also makes it easier to publish more bad content. The platforms have noticed, and they are starting to push back.
Kevin Indig saw this coming. His recent note about “ slop antibodies ” argued that companies need internal systems that filter out low‑grade AI output before it reaches users. He said the problem is not the tools. It is the people who treat them as production engines instead of editorial assistants.
That same day, Tiffany Hsu of The New York Times reported that Spotify had removed 75 million “bulk uploads, duplicate songs and other ‘spammy’ tracks” and that LinkedIn had tightened its detection systems. The piece made a clear point. Platforms are no longer willing to carry the cost of policing junk created by people who treat generative AI as a volume machine.
A few days earlier, Reece Rogers of Wired had posted that communities like Reddit and Stack Overflow have already introduced rules to limit AI‑generated answers because engagement drops when slop spreads unchecked.
This is the moment when SEOs need to ask a harder question. Are the tools the problem, or are we becoming the tools of our tools?
I’ve watched this cycle before. Fifteen years ago, content mills pumped out human‑written webspam at industrial scale. Google did not ban humans. It improved its systems to reward quality. Today, Google’s guidance on AI content says the same thing. The issue is not whether a machine wrote the words. The issue is whether the content is helpful, reliable, and high quality.
That should sound familiar to anyone who has worked in Your‑Money‑or‑Your‑Life categories . Years ago, my team used a tool to optimize and distribute press releases for an online financial newsletter. One release about under‑the‑radar micro‑cap stocks generated a wave of new subscribers. Another release celebrating the newsletter’s anniversary generated none. Same client. Same agency. Same tool. The difference was the content. Readers cared about one and ignored the other.
Tools amplify what you feed them. They do not fix it.
So, the fight over slop is really a fight over judgment. When tools get stronger, the burden on the people using them gets heavier. That is not a modern problem. It is an old one, and earlier thinkers wrestled with the same question long before any of us were optimizing content for search.
That’s why a debate between Henry David Thoreau and Ralph Waldo Emerson still matters. Thoreau warned that people become the tools of their tools. Emerson argued that if you build something genuinely better, the world will beat a path to your door. Both perspectives are alive in today’s AI moment. One warns against surrendering judgment. The other reminds us that great work still wins.
My view is that SEOs are at a crossroads. Black hat practitioners will try to play cat‑and‑mouse with Google for another round or two, but the slop backlash signals that their runway is shrinking. White hat SEOs have a different opportunity. They can use AI to raise the standard of their work instead of lowering it.
The platforms have drawn a line. They are not rejecting AI. They are rejecting slop. SEOs who treat AI as a shortcut will find themselves on the wrong side of that line. SEOs who treat AI as an assistant will find new ways to build better mousetraps.
And when you build something better, the world still beats a path to your door.
